headings.text: AI as a "megamachine" with global effects

html:
The big picture

AI is usually pictured as something immaterial: software "in the cloud" that thinks by itself. This unit takes that picture apart with Kate Crawford's claim that AI is neither artificial nor intelligent. It is not artificial because it is a megamachine: it runs on industrial infrastructure, global supply chains, minerals, water and energy, and the costs of these land unevenly across the world. It is not intelligent on its own because it depends on human labour at every stage: ghost work such as image tagging and content moderation, often underpaid and hidden behind intransparent contract chains, and fauxtomation, where work is not replaced but redistributed and made invisible. The lecture also asks the reverse question: how AI changes jobs (McKinsey's human-agent-robot partnerships, the IMF's exposure and complementarity). It ends with AI's growing energy consumption and the protests against data centres. The common thread with Unit 2: like cars, AI only works inside an infrastructure, and someone always pays for it.

In today's class

  • Questioning the "artificial" in AI…
  • …because it needs human resources
  • …as well as natural resources and energy

Neither artificial nor intelligent

Contemporary forms of artificial intelligence are neither artificial nor intelligent* (Crawford, *Atlas of AI, p. 69, emphasis added)

Intuition: what the two "neithers" mean
  • Not artificial: "artificial" suggests something made out of nothing material, separate from nature. Crawford's point is that AI is made from nature (lithium, cobalt, copper, water for cooling, electricity) and from people (the ones who label data, moderate content, build and maintain hardware). Remove those, and nothing is left.
  • Not intelligent: AI systems do not understand the world on their own; they detect patterns in data that humans collected, sorted and labelled, and they still need humans to correct, check and supervise them. Their "intelligence" is borrowed human intelligence, made at scale.

The slogan is a deliberate provocation: it is not a technical claim that machine learning doesn't work, but a claim about where AI's capacities and costs really come from.

AI as a "megamachine" with global effects

Slide image: a server rack with a tangle of network cables.

  • "a set of technological approaches that depend on industrial infrastructures, supply chains, and human labor that stretch around the globe but are kept opaque" (Kate Crawford, Atlas of AI, p. 48)
  • In addition to energy, long and complex global supply chains that reproduce global inequalities
  • Need for a panoramic, global view of how tech development (including robotics & AI) use resources: metals, water, energy, …
Intuition: the megamachine

A megamachine (the term goes back to Lewis Mumford) is a huge system of people, materials and organisations that works together like one machine, but is too large for anyone to see as a whole. The chatbot on your screen is the visible tip; behind it are mines, chip factories, shipping, data centres, power plants, cooling water, data labellers and moderators, spread across many countries. "Kept opaque" is the key phrase: the system is built so that users see only the tip.

Connection

This is the same move as Unit 2's car example (2 The Bigger Picture – Technology and Society): a technology only functions together with its infrastructure, and once that infrastructure is built it creates path dependencies. Okolo's reading (Class 04 – Human and environmental costs) makes the supply-chain bullet concrete: the critical minerals for chips are mined largely in Global Majority countries, where the harms (polluted water, displaced communities, dangerous and child labour) stay, while the profitable end of the AI value chain sits elsewhere. That is what "reproduce global inequalities" means.

Common mistake: "the cloud" is somewhere else, and weightless

Tempting: AI lives "in the cloud", so its costs are abstract. But the cloud is a metaphor for very physical buildings (data centres) full of chips, connected by cables and drawing power and water from a particular place. Asking "where is this computation happening, and who lives there?" turns an abstract technology into concrete local effects, which is exactly what the data-centre protests at the end of the lecture are about.

How AI affects human labour

How do you think AI/robotics affects human labor?

  • Does AI cost us jobs?
  • Which ones?
  • What kinds of consequences does this have?

Five new jobs for humans if robots take over the world:

  1. Robot singing teacher
  2. Robot plastic surgeon
  3. Robot nurse
  4. Robot travel agent
  5. Organisers/judges for best (robot) in show
Intuition: why the joke list is there

The list (from an article in The Conversation, see Online resources) is tongue-in-cheek, but it makes a serious point: automation does not simply delete jobs, it also creates new ones, and those new jobs often consist of humans serving, fixing and judging the machines. That sets up the rest of the lecture: AI changes what human work looks like and where it is done, and much of the new work is less visible than the old.

How AI changes human labor (or is expected to)

  • McKinsey report (2025): human-agent-robot partnerships

    • Shifting and emerging roles; human skills applied differently
    • Affect greater on e.g. information processing, less on caring/assisting

  • IMF report (2023): exposure and complementarity of/with AI

    • Advanced economies more exposure (but also complementarity)
    • Differences along various axes in how AI changes labor
  • But: does exchanging people for AI actually make sense?
Unclear (slide 6)

"Affect greater on e.g. information processing" is most likely a typo for "Effect greater on …" (the impact of AI is larger on information-processing work, smaller on caring/assisting work). Transcribed as printed.

Intuition: exposure vs. complementarity
  • Exposure = how much of a job's tasks overlap with what AI can do. A clerk who summarises documents is highly exposed; a roofer is not.
  • Complementarity = how likely AI is to support the worker rather than replace them, e.g. because the job also needs responsibility, physical presence or face-to-face judgement. A surgeon or judge is highly exposed (lots of information processing) but also highly complementary (nobody hands the decision to the machine).

High exposure + high complementarity → AI is likely to change the job and possibly make workers more productive. High exposure + low complementarity → the job is at real risk of being replaced. Advanced economies have more office and knowledge work, so they are more exposed, but they also have more of the complementary jobs. That is why the slide says "more exposure (but also complementarity)".

Common mistake: "AI exposure means job loss"

Tempting: if 40% of jobs are "exposed" to AI, 40% of jobs will disappear. But exposure only says that AI touches the job's tasks; whether that means replacement or support depends on complementarity, and on choices by employers and regulators. Both reports describe shifting roles and skills applied differently, not a simple count of jobs lost.

Why ask "does exchanging people for AI actually make sense?"

Because replacing people is often assumed to save money, and that assumption can fail. The AI system has its own costs (licences, computing, energy, integration, errors that need human correction), and the people it replaced often did tacit work nobody had written down, which the system then gets wrong. The Online resources point to a 2026 Forbes piece titled "AI costs more than the people it replaced". The question also links to the next slides: if the AI still needs hidden human labour to work, "replacing" people may only mean moving the work to cheaper, less visible workers elsewhere.

How AI requires human labor to work

  • Much AI work (image tagging, content moderation) relies on un(der)paid labor
  • "Ghost work" and exploitation: financially and psychologically
  • Intransparent contract chains with intermediate companies
Intuition: ghost work

Ghost work (the term is Mary Gray and Siddharth Suri's, 2019) is the human labour that makes AI and online services function but is hidden from users: labelling images so a model can learn what a "cat" or a "pedestrian" is, rating chatbot answers, transcribing audio, and filtering violent or abusive content out of training data and social media feeds. It is usually done as short piecework tasks on online platforms or through outsourcing firms, for low pay and with no job security.

  • Financial exploitation: piece rates that come to a few dollars an hour, tasks that are rejected without pay.
  • Psychological exploitation: content moderators have to look at the worst material on the internet all day, often with little or no mental-health support.
Why do intransparent contract chains matter ethically?

Because they spread out responsibility. A big tech company contracts a platform or outsourcing firm, which contracts another company or individual workers, often in another country. At each step the client can say "these aren't our employees". The workers often don't know whose AI they are training, and the end users don't know the workers exist. Exploitation that would be a scandal inside the company becomes invisible in the chain. This is also the "kept opaque" part of Crawford's megamachine definition, and it returns in Unit 10 on governance and responsibility (Class 10 – Governance and responsibility).

Human labor as a resource

The "Mechanical Turk", an 18th-century chess automaton: the cut-away engraving shows the human chess player hidden inside the machine.

  • They need human labor and human intelligence to work
  • "Fauxtomation": not replacing, but redistributing human work
  • Yet, human work is made invisible (e.g. reCAPTCHA, Amazon, Alexa) and structured according to machine requirements (e.g. time)
Intuition: fauxtomation and the Mechanical Turk

Fauxtomation (faux = fake; the term is Astra Taylor's, used by Crawford) means presenting a process as automated when it actually depends on human work that has been moved somewhere else or onto someone else. The Mechanical Turk in the picture is the perfect image: it seemed to be a machine that played chess, but a human player sat inside. Amazon named its crowd-work platform Amazon Mechanical Turk after it: "artificial artificial intelligence", humans doing the small tasks computers can't.

The slide's examples of invisible work:

  • reCAPTCHA: while "proving you're not a robot", users transcribe words or click on traffic lights and crosswalks, unpaid labelling work that is used to improve automated systems.
  • Amazon: Mechanical Turk workers, and warehouse workers whose pace is set by algorithms.
  • Alexa: human reviewers listened to recordings to improve speech recognition.

"Structured according to machine requirements (e.g. time)" means the work is cut into tiny tasks, timed and paced to fit the system's needs, not the worker's.

Common mistake: "automation replaces human work"

Tempting: an automated system means humans are no longer needed. The fauxtomation point is the reverse: often the human work is still there, but it has been redistributed: to low-paid workers far away (ghost work), or to the customer (self-checkout, reCAPTCHA). The question to ask about any "automated" system is not "is there human labour?" but "whose labour, where, and is it paid and visible?"

Natural resources and energy

AI's (future) energy consumption

"Energy Forecast": energy consumption in TWh/year from 2010 to 2030. Blue: total energy use (data centres, production of ICT, networks wireless & wired, consumer devices — phones & computers); orange: AI's share in total energy use.

Read off the graph (approximate): the total rises from about 2,200 TWh/year in 2010 to about 5,800 in 2025 and about 12,000 in 2030; the orange AI band is thin until 2020 and then grows to roughly 3,500–4,000 TWh/year by 2030.

Unclear (slide 9)

The slide gives no source or date for the graph, and the axis label reads "Twh/year" (should be TWh/year, terawatt-hours per year). The "Graph AI energy use" link in the Online resources points to a 2019 article in Frontiers in Neuroscience, so this is most likely a 2019 projection. Its scope is all ICT (including device production, networks and consumer devices), which is much broader than data centres alone. Compare Crownhart's figure in the Class 04 reading of up to 945 TWh/year for data centres by 2030. The two numbers measure different things and come from different years; which figure, if any, the mini-test expects is not stated.

Intuition: what a terawatt-hour is

1 TWh = 10^{12} Wh = one billion kWh. A typical household in Austria uses a few thousand kWh per year, so 1 TWh/year is roughly the electricity of a few hundred thousand households. Global electricity use is in the order of tens of thousands of TWh/year, so a forecast in the thousands of TWh for ICT is a large share of the world's electricity.

Worked example: where does AI's energy go?

Question: Crownhart says a single chatbot query uses about 0.3 Wh. Is the problem our individual queries?

  1. Check the single number: a 1,000 W microwave running for 1 s uses 1000\,\text{W} \times \tfrac{1}{3600}\,\text{h} \approx 0.28\,\text{Wh}, so "about a second of microwave" matches 0.3 Wh.
  2. Scale it up (hypothetical volume): say 1 billion queries per day: 10^9 \times 0.3\,\text{Wh} = 3\times10^8\,\text{Wh} = 300\,\text{MWh} per day; over a year 300\,\text{MWh} \times 365 \approx 110\,\text{GWh} \approx 0.11\,\text{TWh}.
  3. Compare with the system: 0.11 TWh is about one ten-thousandth of 945 TWh.
  4. Conclusion: everyday text queries are not where the big numbers come from. The big numbers come from the infrastructure as a whole: training ever larger models, energy-heavy uses (video generation, long reasoning sessions), everything else running in data centres and the expected growth. That is Crownhart's argument for putting responsibility on companies and regulators rather than on individual users, and it fits the lecture's "panoramic view".

Data centre protests

Slide: a collage of headlines and a photo of protesters holding a banner reading "DATA CENTRES ARE ENERGY VAMPIRES".

  • "Hundreds protest Google data centre planned for small Austrian town" (Euronews)
  • "Data center opponents stage 142 protests across 42 US states" (Reuters)
  • "Community Backlash to AI Data Centers Is Growing Across the U.S." (Time)
  • "Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam as Europe's backlash spreads" (AP News)
Intuition: why local communities protest

A data centre is a building full of servers that run cloud services and AI. A large one draws as much electricity as a small city, needs water or other cooling for its heat, occupies land and often brings few local jobs once it is built. Communities object because they bear these local costs (strain on the power grid and possibly higher prices, water use, land, noise) while the benefits go to distant companies and users. This is the megamachine made visible in one place: the "opaque" infrastructure suddenly has a street address.

"For one day, we'll become your AI"

Slide: a video still of a group of people standing behind a laptop, subtitled "For one day, we'll become your AI."

Unclear (slide 11)

The slide shows only a video still, with no title or source. The Online resources list "Quili/AI for a day: https://www.quili.ai", so this is most likely the Quili.AI campaign: on 31 January 2026, prompts sent to Quili.AI were answered for 24 hours by residents of Quilicura, Chile, instead of a language model, to draw attention to the water used by AI data centres. What was said about it in class is not on the slides.

Connection

The campaign joins the two halves of the lecture: it makes the hidden human work behind an "AI" answer literal (people answering the prompts), and it was framed around the natural resources (water) that real AI uses.

Terms

  • "Neither artificial nor intelligent" — Crawford's claim that AI depends on material resources and human labour (not artificial) and on human-made data and supervision (not intelligent on its own).
  • Megamachine — AI as a global system of infrastructures, supply chains and human labour that is kept opaque to users (Crawford, after Mumford).
  • Supply chain — the chain of extraction, manufacturing and transport that produces AI hardware; for AI it is long, global and reproduces inequalities.
  • Human-agent-robot partnerships — McKinsey's (2025) picture of work in which humans, AI agents and robots share tasks; roles shift and human skills are applied differently.
  • Exposure (to AI) — how much of a job's tasks overlap with what AI can do (IMF 2023).
  • Complementarity (with AI) — how likely AI is to support rather than replace a worker in that job (IMF 2023).
  • Ghost work — hidden, often underpaid human work such as image tagging and content moderation that AI depends on (Gray & Suri).
  • Intransparent contract chains — chains of intermediate companies between tech firms and workers, which hide who is responsible for working conditions.
  • Fauxtomation — presenting work as automated while it is actually redistributed to (often invisible) humans.
  • Data centre — a building full of servers that runs cloud services and AI; a major user of electricity, water and land.
  • TWh/year — terawatt-hours per year (10^{12} Wh), the unit for national- and global-scale energy use.

Watch next

  • Rocks, Flesh, and Rockets: A Political Ecology of AI — Digital Humanism (TU Wien DIGHUM lecture, filmed). Kate Crawford herself walks through Atlas of AI's argument about the environmental, data and labour costs of AI; it answers Why do intransparent contract chains matter? and puts the megamachine idea in her own words.
  • Why are AI data centers using so much electricity? — TED-Ed (Sajan Saini). An animated explainer of what a data centre is, why it needs so much power and cooling, and whether efficiency can keep up; goes with the energy forecast and the data-centre protests.

(First title and channel confirmed via YouTube's oEmbed data; the second is search-verified, and the TED page responded but its title could not be read automatically.)
